title: Window Performance Explorer
description: Students will analyze (Bloom Level 4, Analyze) how glazing type, coating, and gas fill change U-factor, SHGC, and inside surface temperature, and will judge (Bloom Level 5, Evaluate) which window suits a north wall and a south wall in Minneapolis.
creator: The Science of the Built Environment
author: Dan McCreary
subject: The Science of the Built Environment
chapter_title: Cladding, Windows, Doors, and Air Sealing

pedagogical.learningObjective: Analyze how glazing, coating, gas fill, and frame change U-factor, SHGC, and inside surface temperature, and judge which window suits a north and a south wall in Minneapolis.
recommendedUsage: Start with the default window: double pane, no coating, air fill, vinyl frame, -10 °F outdoors, 40 percent indoor relative humidity, north wall. The room is held at 70 °F, as in the chapter's worked example.

Change one option at a time (glazing, coating, gas, or frame) and watch the three gauges, the temperature profile, and the thermometer update. Hover over a pane, gap, coating, spacer, frame, gauge, or the thermometer to read its role.
Slide the outdoor temperature and the indoor relative humidity. The thermometer turns red and a condensation message appears when the inside glass is colder than the dew point of the room air.
Switch between North and South and read the recommendation line. Try to find the lowest-cost option that suits each wall.
activities: Warm-up (5 min): Students reproduce the chapter's worked example by setting Window A (double clear, vinyl) and Window B (double low-E surface 3, argon, fiberglass) at -10 °F and 40 percent humidity, and compare the glass temperatures.
Explore (10 min): Students raise the humidity until each window starts to condense and record the humidity at which the change happens for three different windows.
Judge (10 min): Students pick one window for a north wall and one for a south wall, justify each using U-factor and SHGC, and compare their picks with a partner.
assessment: Students explain in two sentences why a low-E coating on surface 3 is a better choice than surface 2 for a south wall in a heating climate.
Students explain why the real condensation risk is greater than the thermometer shows, using the cold glass edge.
